ARG.story:
The largest part of Argentina's record is the taking of children by the state. Under the military government of 1976 to 1983, babies seized with their detained parents or born to prisoners in secret detention centres were given to military families and regime allies and registered as their biological children. The national truth commission CONADEP reported in 1984 that no fewer than 200 children under 15 had been kidnapped. In 2012 a federal court in Buenos Aires found that the junta had run a systematic plan to take these children; it sentenced former dictator Jorge Videla to 50 years. Through Operation Condor, the joint action of the region's security forces, a pregnant woman detained in Buenos Aires in 1976 was moved to Montevideo, and her baby was given to a Uruguayan police officer's family.

The Grandmothers of Plaza de Mayo were founded in 1977, and their work led to the creation of the National Bank of Genetic Data, which matches DNA to families. About 500 children are estimated to have been taken. The Grandmothers had found 140 by July 2025; many of those found had not known they were adopted.

In the Catholic Church, Argentina has both received and sent accused clergy. Fr Nicola Corradi was accused at the Provolo school for deaf children in Verona in 2009 and went on working at the same order's school in Luján de Cuyo, Mendoza. A Mendoza court convicted him and two other staff in 2019 of abusing children there between 2004 and 2016. Bishop Gustavo Zanchetta of Orán was given a Vatican post in 2017 after clergy complaints; his victims, in a 2022 conviction, were adult seminarians. The newspaper La Nación reported that at least five Argentine priests accused of abuse or crimes against humanity had sheltered in Paraguay.

Sex trafficking runs through brothel networks, and the US State Department reported in 2025 that Bolivian women and girls are exploited in sex trafficking in Argentina. The case of a young woman abducted in Tucumán in 2002 exposed a network that also trafficked minors; after a court acquitted all 13 defendants in 2012, the province's Supreme Court found 10 guilty in 2013. Campaigners said police were often paid to protect such rings.

Identification of the stolen children continues, with most of the estimated 500 still not found. How many children the trafficking networks reach is not counted in this record.

BGR.story:
Bulgaria's record has two main parts: the sale of Bulgarian girls for sex at home and in Western Europe, and the hosting of child sexual abuse material on Bulgarian servers.

The US State Department reported in 2025 that traffickers exploit Bulgarian women and girls in sex trafficking throughout Western Europe and inside Bulgaria, in Sofia, resort areas and border towns. It cited a UN special rapporteur, an independent expert appointed by the UN, who found that sexual exploitation of children, including possible sex trafficking, was widespread among children living in government-run institutions. The same report lists forced marriages involving Roma and people from countries outside the EU. Children in state care are therefore one of the groups traffickers reach.

Cases rarely end in prison. The report counts 31 traffickers convicted, of whom eight received prison sentences, and describes corruption in the police and courts and impunity for complicit officials as pervasive. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime rates state-embedded criminal actors in Bulgaria at 7.5 out of 10.

Bulgaria is also where much abuse material is stored. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation, a British group that finds and removes such material, acted on 87,959 web addresses hosted in Bulgaria, 28 percent of its total, up from a 9 percent share in 2024; it said a few particular sites drove the rise. Bulgarian cybercrime police have also taken part in takedowns: in Operation Blackwrist, they took down the servers of a subscription site showing the abuse of boys in Thailand.

Bulgaria has sent children abroad for adoption for decades: 5,067 between 2003 and 2022 by one researcher's count, and 2,649 adopted from Sofia received US visas between 1994 and 2014. It remains open to foreign adoption.

The exploitation of girls abroad and in state institutions continues as of 2025, and Bulgaria's share of hosted abuse material rose sharply that year.

DZA.story:
This map holds no documented case, network or cross-border flow of child sexual abuse or trafficking in Algeria. The figures that exist are broad estimates. The US State Department placed Algeria on its Tier 2 Watch List in 2025, one level above the lowest rating. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime scores the country's human trafficking market 4 out of 10 and state-embedded criminal actors 7.5. Walk Free estimates 84,000 people in modern slavery, counting all ages and forms. In 2024 the US National Center for Missing and Exploited Children received 186,589 reports of suspected online child sexual abuse traced to Algeria, 398.6 per 100,000 people.

The research group Childlight found in 2026 that the Middle East and North Africa has no representative survey data on online child sexual exploitation, so how many Algerian children are affected is not known.

CAN.story:
Most of Canada's record concerns abuse in institutions that held children away from their families, many run by churches with government money. The largest was the Indian Residential School system, federally funded schools run by churches to assimilate First Nations, Métis and Inuit children. About 150,000 children attended, and tens of thousands of claims of sexual and serious physical abuse were compensated under a 2007 settlement. About 80,000 children were also sent from Britain by 1920 under migration schemes; the inquiry for England and Wales found in 2018 that the Fairbridge Society failed to respond to sexual abuse allegations at its Canadian schools.

When abuse was reported, the orders involved and sometimes officials protected the abusers. At Mount Cashel, a St John's orphanage run by the Christian Brothers, a Catholic teaching order, the police chief ended an investigation in December 1975 after two Brothers admitted molestation; no charges were laid and four Brothers were moved out of the province. In the Arctic, priests of the Oblates, a Catholic missionary order, abused Inuit children and then left the country. Fr Eric Dejaeger fled to Belgium in 1995 as he was about to be charged and was sentenced in 2015 for 32 offences in Igloolik. Fr Johannes Rivoire left for France in 1993; France refused extradition, and he died there in 2024 without trial after a church-commissioned review concluded he had assaulted six children.

Canada began official inquiries early. The Hughes Royal Commission reported in 1991 that police and the justice department had not handled the Mount Cashel files normally. A 1997 law lets Canada prosecute its citizens for child sex offences abroad.

The sale of children for sex is mostly domestic. Statistics Canada reported that police recorded 4,543 trafficking incidents from 2013 to 2023; about 23 percent of victims were under 18 and 91 percent knew their trafficker. A Quebec legislative commission estimated in 2020 about 600 strip clubs, massage parlours and similar places where men could find a teenager for sex. A Canadian firm was also a large seller of abuse material. Azov Films in Toronto sold films made in Ukraine, Romania and Germany to over 50 countries, and the investigation led to 348 arrests.

The institutional abuse is now largely the subject of settlements and inquiries. Trafficking of girls inside Canada continues, and only 10 percent of completed adult court cases with a trafficking charge ended in a guilty decision.

COL.story:
The largest part of Colombia's record is the recruitment of children by armed groups and the sexual abuse of recruited girls. The Truth Commission, an official body on the armed conflict, documented in 2022 that guerrillas, paramilitary groups and in some cases state security forces recruited 16,238 children between 1990 and 2017, and estimated the real number at 27,101 to 40,828. It found that recruited girls were forced to use contraception and to have abortions and were raped. The Special Jurisdiction for Peace, a court for crimes of the conflict, has indicted former commanders of the FARC-EP guerrilla over 18,677 identified victims of recruitment. Groups that remain armed continue the abuse. The UN verified sexual violence against 33 girls in 2024, by the ELN guerrilla, FARC dissident groups and the armed group Clan del Golfo.

Girls are also sold for sex, often to foreign men. The US State Department reported in 2025 that sex trafficking of girls is prevalent in tourist areas and extractive zones, where natural resources are taken out. In Cartagena, a woman known as La Madame supplied young women and minors to parties for clients. In Medellín, US men travelled repeatedly to exploit girls; by May 2026 US courts working with Colombian authorities had sentenced ten of them.

The displacement of Venezuelans has added to the supply of victims. The State Department reports that Tren de Aragua, a criminal organisation from Venezuela, and the ELN run sex-trafficking networks in Villa del Rosario, Norte de Santander, that Tren de Aragua moves victims through Cúcuta to Argentina, Ecuador and Peru, and that traffickers recruit Colombian and Venezuelan women and girls into webcam studios, an industry likely worth over $1.2 billion a year. Two complicit officials received plea-deal sentences below the legal minimum.

Colombia has sent many children abroad for adoption and remains open to it, with 20,864 sent between 2003 and 2022 by one researcher's count. A ring exposed in 1981 bought or took poor Andean children and sold them abroad with forged papers, and a Dutch inquiry found in 2021 serious violations in adoptions from countries including Colombia.

Abuse inside the Catholic Church has had no national inquiry. In 2020 the Constitutional Court, acting on a journalist's petition, ordered the Archdiocese of Medellín to release records on 43 priests.

Recruitment and sexual violence by armed groups and the trafficking of girls continue as of 2024 and 2025. The scale of abuse in the church is not known.

FRA.story:
France's record is led by abuse in institutions that had authority over children, above all the Catholic Church. The Sauvé commission, set up by the bishops, estimated in 2021 from a population survey that about 216,000 people had been abused as minors by clergy and religious from 1950 to 2020 and called the causes systemic. In Lyon, Fr Bernard Preynat was accused of abusing about 80 Scouts between 1971 and 1991 and was convicted in 2020 only for 10 minors, because many cases were past the legal time limit; Cardinal Philippe Barbarin was convicted of not reporting him, then acquitted on appeal.

The same failures appear in sport, medicine and state care. A parliamentary inquiry in 2024 found that the sports ministry had handled over 1,800 reports, eight in ten involving minors, and that background checks required since 2006 worked only from 2021. The surgeon Joël Le Scouarnec abused 299 victims, mostly patients, from 1989 to 2014; after the FBI traced his downloading of abuse images, a 2005 conviction brought no restriction on his practice, and a hospital hired him in 2008 knowing of it. A 2025 parliamentary report estimated that about 15,000 children in the care of departmental child welfare services are victims of prostitution. A government commission estimated in 2023 that 160,000 children suffer sexual violence each year.

France has also received children through adoption channels later found to be fraudulent. It took in 11,165 South Korean children from 1968 to 2008, adoptions in which South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found state-enabled fraud; Guatemalan and Salvadoran children taken by those countries' armies were also adopted to France. In 2024 the government acknowledged that it had long known of illicit practices of a systemic nature in intercountry adoption.

French men abroad are the accused in several records. Boys in a camp in Bangui said French soldiers of Operation Sangaris abused them in 2013 and 2014; French judges dismissed the case in 2018. The US State Department reports that tourists, often French, exploit children in Madagascar.

As of the 2023 commission report, rape of a minor could not be prosecuted more than 30 years after the victim turned 18, though a 2021 law lets the limit restart if the offender abuses another child. The prostitution of children in state care was still reported in 2025, and France's share of abuse material hosted online rose from 1 percent in 2024 to 7 percent in 2025.

GNQ.story:
The one documented link between Equatorial Guinea and child sexual abuse on this map lies outside the country, through its soldiers. A UN-appointed panel chaired by Marie Deschamps reported in 2015 on accounts by boys aged about 8 to 13, sheltering at a camp in Bangui, Central African Republic, that soldiers had sexually abused them between December 2013 and June 2014, often in exchange for food or money. Most of the accused were French, and the boys also named Chadian and Equatorial Guinean troops of MISCA, the African-led force then in the country. The panel called the UN's handling a gross institutional failure.

Inside the country little is counted. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime rates state-embedded criminal actors at 9 out of 10 and the country's resilience to organised crime at 2.08. Walk Free estimates 11,000 people in modern slavery. The research group Childlight found in 2026 that West and Central Africa has no representative survey data on online child sexual exploitation, so the size of abuse inside Equatorial Guinea is not known.

HTI.story:
In the Haitian record, children are exploited mostly after being separated from their parents: sent to work in other households, placed in orphanages, recruited by gangs, or sent abroad for adoption. The US State Department reported in 2025 that a large share of trafficking cases involve restavek children, children sent to live with host families as unpaid domestic workers, who are often physically abused; displacement from Port-au-Prince increased their risk of sexual exploitation.

Armed gangs have become a main source of sexual violence against children. The UN verified sexual violence against 566 children in 2024, 523 of them girls, up from 41 girls in 2023, and attributed 411 of the cases to the Viv Ansanm gang coalition. Gangs also exploit girls in sex trafficking, and observers report police and immigration officials complicit at the border with the Dominican Republic.

Orphanages are run largely on foreign money. The charity Lumos found in 2017 that at least US$70 million a year went to about a third of Haiti's orphanages, that 92 percent of funders were from the United States and 90 percent faith-based, and that only 15 percent of orphanages were registered. It found that donations drive the opening of orphanages, some run for profit, which recruit children away from families. When Haiti's social welfare agency assessed more than 750 orphanages, it identified 3,019 potential trafficking victims inside them.

Adoption abroad drew on the same separation of children from families. Haiti sent 13,986 children abroad between 2003 and 2022 by one researcher's count. In 2007 a centre was forced to return 47 children to parents it had misled with payments, and after the 2010 earthquake members of an Idaho Baptist group were arrested trying to take 33 children into the Dominican Republic.

Foreign peacekeepers also exploited children. The UN's internal investigators found that sexual abuse of children by the Sri Lankan contingent of the UN mission was frequent and took place at almost every site where it was deployed; the Associated Press found in 2017 that at least 134 of its soldiers had exploited at least nine children between 2004 and 2007. 108 were sent home, Sri Lankan authorities judged the acts consensual, and none was jailed.

Gang sexual violence against children rose sharply in 2024 and continues. The State Department did not give Haiti a ranking in 2025, treating it as a special case.

ISR.story:
In the cases on record, Israel appears mainly as a refuge for people accused of abusing children elsewhere, and as a country where officials and communities have protected them. In March 2008 the Adass Israel School, an ultra-Orthodox school in Melbourne, paid for a 1:20 a.m. flight to Israel for its headmistress, Malka Leifer, after abuse allegations and without telling police. Australia sought her from 2014. In Israel, deputy health minister Yaakov Litzman pressured ministry staff to change psychiatric evaluations so she would appear unfit for extradition, and her lawyers sought more than 70 hearings and appeals. She was extradited in 2021 and convicted in Melbourne in 2023 of 18 charges including rape. Litzman admitted breach of trust in a 2022 plea deal and received eight months' probation. A Russian Orthodox priest, Gleb Grozovsky, also fled to Israel in 2013 after a criminal case was opened in St Petersburg; in his case Israel detained and extradited him.

In Haredi (ultra-Orthodox) communities, the principle of mesirah, which forbids informing on a fellow Jew to secular authorities, has been documented as discouraging reports of abuse in Israel, as in Melbourne and Brooklyn. The sect Lev Tahor, founded in Israel in 1988, is accused of child abuse and forced marriage of teenage girls; its leaders were convicted in the United States in 2021 of kidnapping two children.

The conflict with Palestinians is a second part of the record. The UN Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory and Israel found in June 2024 that Israeli security forces subjected Palestinians to sexual and gender-based violence, including forced public nudity and sexualised torture, and targeted men and boys in particular ways. It also found that sexual violence was committed during the 7 October 2023 attacks, when 252 people, including 36 children, were taken hostage.

On other forms the record is thin. The US National Center for Missing and Exploited Children received 27,575 reports of suspected online child sexual abuse traced to Israel in 2024, and the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime scores the human trafficking market 6.5 out of 10. How often accused people from abroad still find shelter in Israel is not counted.

KGZ.story:
This map holds no documented case or network of child sexual abuse in Kyrgyzstan. Its one entry concerns adoption: Kyrgyzstan suspended intercountry adoption in 2009, and the US State Department issued an adoption alert about the suspension in April 2010.

The broader measures cover all forms of trafficking and are not broken down for children. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime scores the human trafficking market 7 out of 10 and state-embedded criminal actors 8.5. The US State Department placed Kyrgyzstan on its Tier 2 Watch List in 2025, one level above the lowest. Walk Free estimates 57,000 people in modern slavery, 8.7 per 1,000, counting all ages and forms. How many of them are children, and how many are sexually exploited, is not recorded here.

LUX.story:
Luxembourg appears on this map mainly as a country that received adopted children. It took in 561 children from South Korea between 1984 and 2008. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found state-enabled fraud in overseas adoptions, including children falsely registered as orphans and identities swapped by the four agencies that sent them.

The map has no documented case of child sexual abuse or trafficking inside Luxembourg. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime rates state-embedded criminal actors at 1 out of 10, the lowest score, and the US State Department ranks Luxembourg in Tier 1. In 2024 the US National Center for Missing and Exploited Children received 1,684 reports of suspected online child sexual abuse traced to Luxembourg, 248.7 per 100,000 people. Whether any of the Korean adoptions to Luxembourg involved fraud has not been examined in this record.

MLI.story:
In Mali, the documented sexual abuse and abduction of children takes place mostly in the armed conflict. The UN verified the rape of 32 girls in 2024. It could not identify the perpetrators in 22 cases; the others were attributed to the Islamic State in the Greater Sahara (4), the armed group JNIM (3), the Malian armed forces (2) and the militia Ganda Lassal Izo (1). The UN also verified the abduction of 119 children that year, 4 of them by foreign security personnel. In 2023 it verified the rape of 15 girls, 4 of them by the Malian armed forces. The record therefore includes abuse by the state's own forces.

Prosecution has been limited. In 2024 the International Criminal Court convicted Al Hassan Ag Abdoul Aziz, of the Islamic police that the armed groups Ansar Eddine and AQIM ran in Timbuktu in 2012 and 2013, of torture and persecution, but acquitted him of rape and sexual slavery, charges that included forced marriages of women and girls.

Mali is also a source and a destination in regional trafficking. Some of the more than 300 boys and men freed in 2019 from a building in Kaduna, Nigeria, signed as an Islamic studies centre, had been brought from Mali; local media reported they were tortured, starved and sexually abused, and seven people were arrested. The US State Department reports that Nigerian networks move women and girls to mining regions that include Mali, and that women and girls from Mali are among those exploited at gold-mining sites in Senegal.

The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime rates Mali's resilience to organised crime at 2.08 out of 10. The UN figures count only cases it could verify, and the research group Childlight found no representative survey data for West and Central Africa, so the full scale is not known.

NER.story:
The documented record for Niger concerns the abduction of children by armed groups. The UN verified the abduction of 202 children in 2024, 102 of them girls, and sexual violence against five girls. Most abductions (163) were by perpetrators the UN could not identify; others were by Boko Haram, also called JAS (35), by ISWAP (2) and by the Islamic State in the Greater Sahara (2). Boko Haram and ISWAP operate across the Lake Chad basin, which includes Niger, and in Nigeria they have abducted schoolgirls and forced girls into marriage. In 2023 the UN verified sexual violence against eight girls in Niger, one of the cases by the country's own security forces.

Other forms are not documented on this map. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime scores the human trafficking market 8 out of 10 and state-embedded criminal actors 8, and the US State Department placed Niger on its Tier 2 Watch List in 2025. The UN counts only cases it can verify, and Childlight found no representative survey data on online abuse for West and Central Africa.

PAK.story:
Three forms of child sexual exploitation are documented in Pakistan: abuse of pupils by clerics in madrassas (Islamic religious schools), abuse by local gangs who film children and blackmail their families, and the sale of poor girls as brides to men in China. In all three, police or officials failed to act.

The madrassas hold the largest number of children: more than 22,000 are registered, with at least 2 million pupils. An Associated Press investigation in 2017 found sexual abuse by clerics pervasive and seldom prosecuted, and a follow-up in 2020 based on police reports found the same. Police are often paid not to register cases, and poor families are pressed to forgive the cleric in exchange for money, which Pakistani law allows; in one case a teacher who confessed was freed after the mother accepted $300. Police told the AP that clerics are almost never convicted.

In Hussain Khanwala village in Kasur district, a gang filmed the sexual abuse of children and blackmailed their parents with the videos; Pakistani media put the number of children at 280 to 300. Police acted in 2015 only after clashes between relatives and the authorities drew media attention, and police and a local provincial assembly member were alleged to have tried to cover it up. A Punjab government investigation team confirmed 19 complaints and charged 17 people; two men received life sentences in 2016 and 12 others were acquitted.

Brokers target poor Christian communities to sell girls and women to Chinese men as brides. A Federal Investigation Agency list obtained by the AP named 629 sold from 2018 to mid-2019. Officials told the AP the investigation largely stopped after pressure from officials worried about ties with Beijing, and a court acquitted 31 Chinese nationals in 2019 after witnesses were threatened or bribed. The US State Department reported in 2025 that hundreds of those sent to China reported being forced into commercial sex. Pakistan is also a destination for Bangladeshi girls trafficked for sex.

In 2024 the US National Center for Missing and Exploited Children received 848,261 reports of suspected online child sexual abuse traced to Pakistan. Prosecution of clerics remains rare, and Childlight found no representative survey data on online abuse for South Asia.

PRT.story:
Portugal's record centres on two institutions that held children: Casa Pia, a state institution caring for about 4,500 children, and the Catholic Church.

At Casa Pia, boys in state care were abused by staff and procured for other men. The abuse is said to have begun in the mid-1970s and became public in 2002. In 2010 a Lisbon court convicted six men. The former Casa Pia driver Carlos Silvino received 18 years after confessing to 639 charges of abusing boys or procuring them for others. The others convicted were a television presenter, a doctor, a retired ambassador, a lawyer and a former Casa Pia governor; all except Silvino denied the charges.

The men's standing and the institution's inaction kept the abuse going for decades. A teacher reportedly told Casa Pia leaders and police about abuse from 1975, and police accused a caretaker in 1981, without legal action. The ambassador, Jorge Ritto, had been removed as consul in Stuttgart around 1969 to 1971 after a complaint about an under-age boy, but stayed in the diplomatic service. On this map, 27 years passed between the first report and the first action.

In the Catholic Church, an independent commission set up by the bishops and led by the child psychiatrist Pedro Strecht reported in 2023, after hearing more than 500 survivors, that at least 4,815 children had been abused since 1950. Most offences were past the legal time limit, and 25 cases were passed to prosecutors.

Portugal also appears in online abuse cases: Portuguese police arrested and charged the administrator of the hidden abuse site Babyheart in 2017 after an international investigation located him there. The US National Center for Missing and Exploited Children received 37,529 reports of suspected online child sexual abuse traced to Portugal in 2024.

The Casa Pia convictions and the church commission recorded what happened. Because of time limits, most of the abuse found in the church will not reach a court.

SDN.story:
In Sudan, the documented sexual abuse of children is part of the war between the army and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), a paramilitary force, which began in April 2023. The UN's independent fact-finding mission for Sudan found in 2024 that rape and gang rape were widespread, committed mostly by men in RSF uniform and allied militias, and that victims included girls as young as 8. It found that the RSF's abduction and detention of women and girls for sexual purposes amounted to sexual slavery. The Sudanese Armed Forces were responsible for some cases.

The UN Secretary-General's verified counts show the same pattern. The UN verified sexual violence against 114 girls in 2023, 57 of the cases by the RSF, and against 74 children in 2024, 54 by the RSF and 9 by militias allied to it, and listed the RSF for the rape and abduction of children. Foreign forces have also been named: in an earlier report the UN attributed 4 of 35 verified cases of sexual violence against girls aged 12 to 17 in Sudan to the Chadian National Army.

Sudan is also a destination for trafficked girls. The US State Department reported in 2025 that traffickers exploit Ethiopian girls in domestic servitude and sex trafficking in neighbouring countries, particularly Djibouti and Sudan, sometimes using drugs to control them. The State Department ranks Sudan in Tier 3, its lowest rating, and the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime scores its human trafficking market 8.5 out of 10.

The UN counts only cases it can verify, and the research group Childlight found no representative survey data on online abuse for the region, so the number of children abused in the war is not known. The sexual violence was continuing when the UN reported in 2024.

SVK.story:
The documented record for Slovakia concerns abuse in the Catholic Church, and it comes from the church itself. In March 2024 the Slovak bishops' commission for the protection of minors published its first evaluation report, counting complaints made since 1990. Of 68 complaints, 39 were confirmed, 17 remained open, 7 could not be resolved and 5 were not confirmed. The confirmed cases involved more than 44 victims. Fifty complaints concerned dioceses of the Latin (Roman) rite, three concerned Greek Catholic eparchies, the dioceses of the Eastern-rite Catholic church, and 15 concerned religious orders. No independent or state inquiry is recorded.

On other forms the record is thin. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime scores the human trafficking market 5.5 out of 10 and state-embedded criminal actors 7. Walk Free estimates 42,000 people in modern slavery, counting all ages and forms. In 2024 the US National Center for Missing and Exploited Children received 17,532 reports of suspected online child sexual abuse traced to Slovakia, 323.3 per 100,000 people. A report based on complaints to the church counts only those who came forward.

TLS.story:
Timor-Leste's record has two parts: the removal of children to Indonesia during the occupation, and sexual abuse of children by Catholic clergy that the church kept from the public.

The Commission for Reception, Truth and Reconciliation (CAVR), the country's truth commission, reported in 2005 that at least 4,000 children were forcibly taken from their families and moved illegally to Indonesia between 1975 and 1999. Indonesian military units took some and used them as child soldiers or servants; Islamic organisations took others and converted them. The children were often renamed and lost contact with their families. The commission called separating a child from their identity, culture, religion or language a grave breach of the Fourth Geneva Convention. It and a joint Indonesia–Timor-Leste commission recommended a body to search for the missing children, and none was created.

In the church, abuse by clergy was first handled in private. Richard Daschbach, a US-born missionary priest, founded the Topu Honis children's shelter in Oecusse in 1992. He admitted abuse to his superiors in 2018 and the Vatican dismissed him from the priesthood that year without telling the public; he was arrested in 2019 and sentenced in 2021 to 12 years, and a report by the Dili archdiocese's Justice and Peace Commission had defended him. Two men told a Dutch magazine in 2022 that Bishop Carlos Ximenes Belo, a Nobel Peace Prize winner, had abused them and other boys in Fatumaca and Dili. The Vatican then confirmed that it had received allegations in 2019 and had imposed sanctions in 2020, including no contact with minors or with Timor-Leste, without disclosing them.

The children taken to Indonesia have never been systematically searched for. How many children were abused by clergy has not been examined by any inquiry.

URY.story:
Uruguay's documented record concerns the taking of children by the military in the 1970s, in cooperation with Argentina's junta under Operation Condor, the joint action of the region's security forces. In 1976 a pregnant 19-year-old Argentine detained in Buenos Aires was moved secretly to Montevideo by Uruguay's Defense Information Service and a joint Argentine–Uruguayan commando. She gave birth in a military hospital, and her baby was taken in December 1976 and left with a police officer's family, who raised her under another identity for 23 years. In Argentina, a court found that the junta ran a systematic plan to take children born to detained mothers, and about 500 are estimated to have been taken.

Uruguay's 1986 Expiry Law, an amnesty for crimes of the dictatorship, was used to close the investigation in 2003. In 2011 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights found Uruguay responsible for the disappearance and the suppression of the child's identity, and ruled the amnesty legally without effect.

The map has no other documented case for Uruguay. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime scores its human trafficking market 3.5 out of 10. How many other children were taken through Uruguay is not recorded here.

YEM.story:
In Yemen, the documented sexual abuse of children is committed mostly by armed forces in the war, including government forces and the police. The UN verified sexual violence against 24 children in 2023, 16 girls and 8 boys, and attributed 20 of the cases to the Yemen Armed Forces and forces allied to them, including 4 by the Yemeni police. In 2024 it verified 11 cases: 2 by the Houthi armed movement, 2 by the Yemen Armed Forces and 7 by affiliated forces, including 4 by the police.

Detention is one setting. The Group of Eminent Experts on Yemen, appointed by the UN Human Rights Council, reported in 2019 that the Security Belt Forces, a force allied to the government, raped four boys and a girl between 2016 and 2019 and committed widespread rape of migrant women, girls and boys at a former facility in Aden. It found that members of the 35th Armoured Brigade raped two boys, that personnel of the United Arab Emirates at Al-Bureiqa raped a boy, and that a 17-year-old boy suffered sexual violence in a Houthi detention site.

Recruitment is another. The Group found credible accounts in 2020 that the Houthis recruited 34 girls aged 13 to 17 between 2015 and 2020, and that 12 of them reportedly suffered sexual violence, forced early marriage linked to their recruitment, or both.

The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime scores Yemen's human trafficking market 9 out of 10 and its resilience to organised crime 1.92. The Group of Eminent Experts said its figures were a small sample, and the research group Childlight found no representative survey data on online abuse for the region, so the extent of abuse is not known.
